title: A Knight Needs a Witness
boundary: Part I, chapter 1: opening portrait, reading habits, armor and helmet, naming Rocinante and Don Quixote, ending with Dulcinea. No later plot revealed.

sources.title: A life rearranged by reading
sources.quote: he sold many an acre of tillageland to buy books of chivalry to read
sources.note: This is an action reported by the narrator, not a direct statement of the gentleman’s feelings. Books of chivalry are romances about knights and idealized adventures. The action supports an inference about his priorities; it does not establish that every reader behaves this way.

sources.title: A test and its aftermath
sources.quote: not caring to try any more experiments with it, he passed it and adopted it as a helmet of the most perfect construction.
sources.note: After a sword test breaks his pasteboard repair, he rebuilds it with iron bars and chooses not to test again. “Most perfect” is the narrator’s report of the adopted assessment, in tension with the testing history. Pasteboard means layers of paper/cardboard; a morion is an open helmet. Preserve the distinction between observation and claimed perfection.

sources.title: A name that makes a claim
sources.quote: a distinguished and full-sounding one, befitting the new order and calling he was about to follow.
sources.note: He spends four days naming his horse Rocinante and then eight naming himself Don Quixote. The chosen words give an ordinary horse and gentleman a grand imagined identity. Diction is purposeful word choice. This English phrasing belongs to John Ormsby’s translation, not Cervantes’s original Spanish.

scenes.title: The door on the cover
scenes.speaker: journal
text: Mr. Hepting sets an old journal on the desk. Its leather cover looks as if it has survived rain, travel, and a serious disagreement with a suitcase zipper.

‘I found this in an airport gift shop in Peru,’ he says. ‘Between the marmalade and the neck pillows. I asked it why boarding groups exist. I was gone three days.’ On the cover, someone has drawn a door. The little brass handle feels surprisingly real.

‘A new question on a new line,’ he says. ‘Then touch the door. It takes you somewhere you can investigate. Answers are your responsibility. So is coming back.’ I write a question. The page smells faintly of oranges. No classmates follow me: this small door is an invitation for one.

choices.label: How much can a name change a person?
choices.response: I write about names. The ink stretches into a narrow road. My own name stays on this side of the cover; the question goes ahead of me.

choices.label: What makes someone a hero before the first adventure?
choices.response: I write about heroes. The door grows tall enough for my shoulders. Somewhere beyond it, somebody is polishing something that squeaks.

choices.label: Can a story change the way we see ordinary things?
choices.response: I write about stories. The little handle warms in my palm. The page turns itself, patiently waiting for me to stop staring and enter.

scenes.title: An appointment with no salary
scenes.speaker: quixote
text: I step into a courtyard in La Mancha, a region of Spain. An older gentleman has placed a rusty helmet beside a pile of books. His horse watches the arrangement with the weary patience of an animal excluded from the planning committee.

‘At last,’ the gentleman says. ‘A chronicler.’ A chronicler records what happens. I explain that I have mostly recorded homework. ‘A promising apprenticeship,’ he says. ‘Will you witness my beginning? The world cannot remember a deed it never hears about.’

He calls himself Don Quixote. He is preparing to become a knight-errant: a wandering knight who seeks adventures and rights wrongs. His armor belonged to his great-grandfather. His confidence is considerably newer. I accept the appointment for this visit. My problem is already clear: can I tell the truth about him without making his hopes into a joke?

choices.label: I ask what he hopes a chronicler can preserve.
choices.response: ‘That I tried,’ he says, then straightens. ‘And my considerable victories, when they become available.’ The second answer stands proudly beside the first. I suspect the first is carrying more weight.

choices.label: I ask who else should be heard.
choices.response: His niece appears at the doorway, carrying folded linen. ‘Someone who knows where the bread is kept,’ she says. Quixote introduces her with affection and immediately promises that glory will not interfere with lunch. She looks unconvinced.

margin.text: A quill appears at the bottom edge of my page. Cervantes peers over it, smiling. “You have met a man and an ambition. Do not confuse either with my narrator. What do you actually know so far?”

followups.q: Can I ask what you intended?
followups.a: “You can ask. But my presence in this margin is an invitation to investigate, not proof of a private intention. Let the words make trouble for your first answer.”

scenes.title: What the books cost
scenes.speaker: niece
text: His niece opens the book-room door. Volumes lean against one another like tired travelers. I imagine a shelf that keeps getting larger while the field outside gets smaller.

‘He reads late,’ she says. ‘And speaks as if a book were giving him instructions.’ Her concern tells me about her perspective. It is not enough, by itself, to prove everything she fears. The journal offers a labelled fragment of the actual opening chapter.

Characterization means how a text builds our understanding of a character through actions, speech, description, and relationships. I need to separate what the passage states from what I infer. My first notebook entry must show that separation.

choices.label: The narrator says he sells farmland for books; I infer that reading has become a powerful priority.
choices.response: The journal underlines “sold” and circles “infer.” The action is evidence; the priority is a defensible interpretation. The niece nods at the detail, then asks whether a powerful priority is always a wise one.

choices.label: Selling land for books suggests devotion and poor judgment; the action supports both, without settling his whole character.
choices.response: I keep admiration and concern on the same line. A concrete action can support more than one inference. The niece is glad I have not made her uncle only a label.

choices.label: The passage proves that reading fiction makes everyone foolish.
choices.response: The journal asks: “Everyone?” One character’s reported action does not establish a universal cause. I mark this as an overclaim and retain the source beside it for review.

scenes.title: What kind of chronicler?
scenes.speaker: quixote
text: Quixote offers me a quill whose feather has survived rather better than its tip. ‘Will your account be grand?’ he asks. His niece stays by the door. Neither wants him to disappear, though they mean different things by disappearing.

I can emphasize his aspiration or the gap between aspiration and household life. Either approach can be honest if I use evidence. The commitment changes whom I speak with and the tone of my account; it earns no correctness points. Praise may keep him listening but hide a problem. Direct skepticism may protect accuracy but close a conversation.

choices.label: I promise to begin with his hope, then test the claims it creates.
choices.response: He smiles. ‘Hope first. Excellent.’ When I add “test,” his smile pauses. He invites me to look at the helmet anyway. My kindness has opened a door; it has not made him agree.

choices.label: I promise to record the ordinary details beside the heroic claims.
choices.response: His niece brings the helmet closer. Quixote looks wounded. ‘Ordinary details are notoriously ordinary.’ I explain that they can reveal what a heroic claim asks us to believe. He lets me stay, though he now watches my quill.

choices.label: I promise to write only the grand parts so he will like my account.
choices.response: He is delighted. The niece withdraws to her work. I have won his approval and made my job harder: an account that cannot mention inconvenient details cannot examine its own claims. I will still have chances to reason carefully.

scenes.title: A helmet of the most perfect construction
scenes.speaker: quixote
text: He raises the repaired helmet. Its paper parts suggest an expensive hat having a difficult morning. ‘I improved it,’ he says. The source card tells a fuller story: his first sword test destroyed a week’s work; after rebuilding with iron bars, he chose not to run another experiment.

I do not repeat the sword test. My appointment is to witness, not to alter the chapter. Instead I set the evidence beside the description “most perfect construction.” Diction is word choice; parody imitates the language or conventions of a genre while exposing their oddities or limits.

Here the grand confidence of knightly preparation sits beside a homemade repair and an avoided test. The comic effect has a cost: he needs this fragile thing to be enough. I choose the sentence that best explains how language produces that effect.

choices.label: “Most perfect” echoes heroic certainty, while the avoided retest makes that certainty comic and questionable.
choices.response: My quill joins a phrase to an action. The diction claims perfection; the testing history unsettles it. This is a specific explanation of parody, not simply a judgment that the man is silly.

choices.label: The grand phrase makes the repair comic; the refused retest also suggests how much he wants his new identity to hold together.
choices.response: I explain the contrast before offering the inference about desire. The ache is an interpretation supported by the action, not a fact the source explicitly announces.

choices.label: “Most perfect” proves that the narrator has certified the helmet safe.
choices.response: I have treated an adopted claim as a successful experiment. The journal points me back to the avoided test. To explain the language, I must notice the tension between these details.

margin.text: Cervantes nudges a comma with his quill. “Paper can be funny. A person needing paper to become steel may be sad. Can your reading make room for both?”

followups.q: Does comedy mean we should despise him?
followups.a: “Laughter can expose a mistake without finishing our judgment of the person. Which detail invites laughter? Which makes that laughter uncomfortable? Try answering separately.”

followups.q: Are all knightly stories being rejected?
followups.a: “A parody can imitate conventions and test them. This scene gives you a failed preparation and extravagant confidence. It does not settle every possible value of every romance.”

scenes.title: Names fit for the road
scenes.speaker: quixote
text: He introduces Rocinante, the horse. Rocinante lowers his head toward a patch of grass. This is not the introduction Quixote had rehearsed.

The source describes the effort to find a distinguished, full-sounding name. Quixote gives himself a grand name too, drawing on the conventions of the knights he has read about. A name can announce an aspiration without proving that the aspiration has been fulfilled.

He looks from the horse to me. ‘When the right name is found, a beginning becomes possible.’ I can hear the hope in his voice. My inference must still account for the gap between his words and the ordinary things around him.

choices.label: The names help him perform a desired identity; ordinary details make that performance both hopeful and doubtful.
choices.response: I write “desired,” not “achieved.” His naming actions support self-invention, and the contrast keeps my conclusion qualified. He enjoys the word “hopeful” and politely declines “doubtful.” Both remain in my notebook.

choices.label: His careful naming shows commitment, but it cannot establish his readiness to be a knight.
choices.response: The inference stays close to the naming effort and admits its limit. I do not deny the commitment; I distinguish commitment from competence. Rocinante continues his own investigation of grass.

choices.label: The new names mean he has already become an accomplished hero.
choices.response: A claim of identity is not evidence of an accomplishment. I cross out “already.” His effort matters, but the source has not yet shown the heroic deeds this sentence assumes.

scenes.title: A hero beside another hero
scenes.speaker: niece
text: The niece walks with me to the gate. ‘If he wants to help people,’ she says, ‘must he first become a character from a book?’ She does not ask me to forbid his dream. She asks what the dream prevents him from seeing.

My journal draws two empty boxes: “this passage” and “another model of heroism.” I can connect Quixote’s preparation to a hero from our epic readings, or keep the comparison at the level of genre. A connection needs a shared feature and a meaningful difference. It should not turn two cultures into one easy rule.
The gate creaks. Soon I must finish the first page. Which connection can I defend with the evidence available?

choices.label: Both epic heroes and Quixote may seek renown; this opening tests heroic preparation through domestic detail and parody.
choices.response: The connection names a shared aspiration and a difference in treatment. I would need a particular epic passage for a fuller comparison. I leave space for one rather than inventing a quotation.

choices.label: A hero’s reputation depends partly on a story being told; here the gap between naming and doing asks the chronicler to examine that reputation.
choices.response: I connect storytelling and heroism through the naming evidence. This is a question to take back to a specific epic, not a claim that every hero or culture values reputation in the same way.

choices.label: This proves Spanish people mock heroes while ancient cultures admire all heroes.
choices.response: Two sweeping claims outrun the scene. A single text and a genre contrast cannot establish what entire cultures believe. I revise toward a named passage, a shared feature, and a limited difference.

margin.text: Cervantes holds the page open, but leaves the road untouched. “Your earlier heroes need not fit in my pocket. Bring a passage when you compare. What changes when a familiar heroic pose is tried in an ordinary courtyard?”

followups.q: Are author and narrator the same voice?
followups.a: “The historical author wrote the novel; a narrator tells it; Quixote speaks and acts within it. My margin visits here are another invented voice. Distinguish whose words you are using before claiming authority.”

scenes.title: The introduction I can sign
scenes.speaker: quixote
text: Quixote stands by the gate, expecting a sentence large enough to march under. I am holding the small beginning I can actually justify. My first question is not completely answered. A name can help someone begin; it cannot do all the work of becoming.

I choose how to introduce him honestly—or how to handle the temptation to flatter him. My evidence and interpretation checkpoints have already earned their credit. His reaction will not change those points. The journal waits for an account I am willing to carry back.
Before I turn the page, I may add a private reflection: what did I discover, and what remains uncertain? The door on the cover is waiting. It requires understanding, not the knight’s approval.

choices.label: I introduce a man seeking heroic purpose, whose books and names outrun his tested equipment.
choices.response: He likes “purpose.” He objects to “outrun.” I read the helmet detail back to him, gently. He does not accept my wording, but he thanks me for staying long enough to find wording worth disputing. My account keeps hope and evidence together.

choices.label: I introduce a would-be knight whose self-invention is exposed by ordinary details, while acknowledging the longing behind it.
choices.response: He folds his hands. ‘Would-be is a thin suit of armor.’ I cannot make the phrase painless. His niece asks me to leave “longing” in. I do. Honesty has cost me easy approval, and allowed a fuller portrait.

choices.label: I introduce an already perfect knight, omitting the evidence that contradicts the claim.
choices.response: He beams, then asks what I thought of the helmet. My sentence has made that question awkward. The journal records my chosen introduction beside my actual evidence: the difference is now visible to me. I can name what needs revision even after failing to say it aloud.

driverQuestions.prompt: Which entry separates evidence from inference?
options: He sells land for books; this suggests that reading has become a priority.
He is heroic because he gives himself a heroic name.
Everyone who reads fiction loses judgment.
driverQuestions.note: The reported sale is evidence. The priority is an inference supported by that action.

driverQuestions.prompt: Why is “most perfect construction” comic in the helmet passage?
options: It is a technical safety certificate.
Grand confidence contrasts with a repair he chooses not to retest.
driverQuestions.note: The grand description and the avoided experiment pull in different directions; connect wording with action.

driverQuestions.prompt: Which reading of the new names is most defensible?
options: The horse shares the knight’s beliefs.
Names perform an aspiration without proving it achieved.
driverQuestions.note: Diction can announce identity. It cannot establish competence or accomplishments that have not been shown.

driverQuestions.prompt: Which comparison should I carry into class?
options: All cultures have the same definition of a hero.
Compare one heroic aspiration across specific passages, and explain a difference in treatment.
driverQuestions.note: A useful comparison preserves specific evidence and differences. Parody can coexist with sympathy.

edition: Miguel de Cervantes, Don Quixote, translated by John Ormsby (1885), Project Gutenberg eBook 996, public domain.
notes: Original dialogue, student appointment, journal magic, and Cervantes margin visits are authored fiction. Labelled source cards alone contain authentic excerpts. Author, narrator, and character voices are distinct. These are episode concepts; a current assigned weekly vocabulary list and class translation were not verified. Read the assigned class text as well. No live AI responses.
